scenario: AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

Answer: <0 or 1>

The Deeper Issue: Your Daughter’s Autonomy (Philosophical Perspective)** Your father’s approach reflects a **traditional, control-driven parenting style** that prioritizes **outcomes over well-being**. Here’s why this matters: - **Forced activities breed resentment.** Studies show that **children who are pressured into sports/hobbies** often develop **anxiety, burnout, or a dislike for the activity** (even if they’re "good at it"). That’s **not selfish**; it’s **protective**. - **People-pleasing vs. self-advocacy.** You’re used to **suppressing your needs** (as a child) but now **struggling with asserting yours** (as a parent). This is a **healthy shift**, but it can feel messy. - **Guilt vs. boundaries.** You’re **guilty for "disappointing" your father** (a common family dynamic) but **angry at his lack of respect for your daughter**. This **internal conflict** is normal but exhausting. **Solution:** Write down: 1. **What you need** (e.g., "My daughter’s happiness > my father’s expectations"). 2. **What you’re afraid of** (e.g., "He’ll think I’m a bad parent"). 3. **What you’re willing to accept** (e.g., "I won’t force her into basketball, but I’ll keep the door open for her to try it later"). --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Not an Asshole)** - **You were not "wrong" for your reaction**—it was a **protest against a harmful dynamic**. - **You were "asshole-adjacent" for the delivery**—but that’s often about **communication style**, not intent. - **You’re not obligated to apologize** if you don’t feel guilty, but a **strategic acknowledgment** (not a full apology) could help long-term. **What to do now:** 1. **Give yourself grace.** You’re navigating **complex emotions**—that’s hard. 2. **Reinforce your daughter’s autonomy.** Let her know: *"Your feelings matter. We’ll do what you want to do."* 3. **Set a boundary with your father.** Not in anger, but **calmly**: *"I won’t force her into anything. Let’s talk about what she enjoys."* 4. **Decide if you want to repair the relationship.** If yes, **apologize for the tone, not the substance**. --- ### **TL;DR:** You’re **not an asshole** for standing up for your daughter. Your reaction was **proportionate to the trigger**, even if the *how* could’ve been smoother. **Not apologizing isn’t assholery—it’s self-respect.** The real question is: *Are you okay with the consequences?* If you prioritize your daughter’s well-being over your father’s approval, that’s **not selfish; it’s parenting**.
